title: "3. Where They Meet"
format:
  html:
    toc: true

> AI has genuinely changed parts of biology. It has changed other parts not at
> all. Knowing which is which is a research skill.

## Learning objectives

1. Name problems where AI has produced real biological advances.
2. Name problems where classical methods remain better.
3. Apply a short test to decide whether your problem suits an AI approach.
4. Explain why interpretability matters more in clinical settings.

## Where it genuinely worked

**Protein structure prediction.** AlphaFold changed this field. The problem had
the exact properties deep learning needs: a large corpus of solved structures,
a well-defined input (sequence) and output (coordinates), and a clear measure
of success. Structures that took years now take hours.

**Basecalling.** Nanopore basecalling is a neural network turning electrical
signal into bases. Accuracy improvements here came from better models, not
better chemistry.

**Variant effect prediction.** Predicting whether a missense variant is
damaging is now dominated by learned models.

**Image-heavy tasks.** Cell segmentation, histopathology screening — anywhere
the input is pixels.

## Where it mostly has not

**Small-sample association studies.** With 338 participants and 4 groups, a
contingency table and Fisher's exact test are the right tools. A neural network
would overfit instantly and tell you less.

**Anything where you must explain the answer.** If a clinician must act on the
output, "the model said so" is not sufficient. A logistic regression with
interpretable coefficients may be worth more than an opaque model that scores
two points higher.

**Problems with a known mechanism.** We understand how sequences align. Use the
algorithm.

**Confounded designs.** No model repairs a broken study. This is the lesson of
the [case study](../4-hands-on/index.qmd) — and it is worth stating plainly:
*AI cannot fix data that never contained the answer.*

## A short test

Before reaching for machine learning, ask:

1. **How many examples do I have?** Hundreds → classical statistics. Tens of
   thousands → ML becomes reasonable.
2. **Do I have trustworthy labels?** ML inherits every bias in your labels.
3. **Do I need to explain the answer?** If yes, weight interpretability
   heavily.
4. **Is there a known mechanism?** If yes, use it.
5. **Would a simple model do?** Try it first. It is your baseline, and it is
   often the winner.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Always fit the simple model first
A logistic regression takes two minutes and gives you a number to beat. If your
deep model cannot beat it, that is the finding — and you learned it cheaply.
:::

## The honest summary

AI is a set of tools with a specific profile: excellent when you have many
examples, a clear objective, and tolerance for opacity. Southern African
genomics research frequently has none of those things — cohorts are small,
questions are causal, and results inform clinical decisions.

That is not a reason to avoid these methods. It is a reason to use them where
they fit, and to be the person in the room who can say why they don't.

::: {.callout-important}
## What we want you to leave with
Not "AI is overhyped" and not "AI will solve this". Both are lazy. The useful
position is: *this problem has these properties, therefore this method* — and
being able to defend that sentence.
:::

## Check yourself

1. You have 200 sequenced isolates and want to predict drug resistance from
   sequence. Neural network or regression? What would you need to change your
   answer?
2. Why is interpretability more valuable in a clinic than in a screening pipeline?
3. Your model beats logistic regression by 1%. Is it better?

Take these into the [exercise](exercise.qmd).
